_README: Every constant this model uses, with its source. Nothing numeric lives in
model.py. Edit here (or override on the CLI) and re-run.
PROVENANCE WARNING, read before trusting any row: the session that built
this had WebFetch and curl blocked by an egress allowlist for every domain
below except the search index itself. Every figure was read out of a search
engine's summary of the page, NOT the page. Rows are tagged with
'confidence'. Re-verify anything tagged 'secondary' against the primary URL
before this model informs a purchase.

electricity._note: Montgomery County MD is Pepco territory (Pepco serves ~567k customers across Montgomery + Prince George's). No county-specific tariff exists; you take Pepco's Maryland rate schedules. A 24/7 inference node is a demand-metered ~100% load-factor customer, which is the best case for amortizing demand charges, so the low end of this band is reachable with competitive supply.

md_commercial_eia_aug2026.source: EIA state commercial average, Aug 2026, via https://energystackhub.com/resources/commercial-electricity-rates-by-state

md_commercial_eia_dec2025.source: EIA report Dec 2025, MD commercial average

md_residential_eia_corrected.source: EIA, after the Maryland PSC forced a correction: https://psc.maryland.gov/news/2026/u-s-eia-corrects-maryland-electricity-price-data/
md_residential_eia_corrected.note: The Mar 2026 report said 35 c/kWh (2nd highest in the US, +89% YoY); corrected to 22.2 c, +17% YoY. Use this for a home office. The episode is also the reason every EIA row here is tagged secondary.

md_industrial_eia.source: EIA report Dec 2025, MD industrial average

pepco_sos_price_to_compare_summer_2026.note: SUPPLY ONLY. Delivery rides on top. Do NOT use as an all-in rate.

pending_risk.note: MD commercial rates already rose ~26% after an early-2026 rate case. EIA also published a bad MD residential number in Mar 2026 (35c, corrected to 22.2c) - see https://psc.maryland.gov/news/2026/u-s-eia-corrects-maryland-electricity-price-data/ - so treat wild MD figures with suspicion.

gpt-5.6-luna.size_note: Parameter count UNDISCLOSED. Third-party '27B dense' and '8.8B dense' claims found in search summaries are unreliable and appear to conflate other model cards. This model deliberately does NOT assume a Luna size; it sizes hardware from a capability-matched OPEN model instead.

deepseek-v4-pro-0813.source: https://artificialanalysis.ai/models/deepseek-v4-pro ; https://deepseek.ai/deepseek-v4 ; weights published 2026-08-13 as 66 fp8 shards, ungated
deepseek-v4-pro-0813.note: THE CAPABILITY MATCH. AA index 53 vs Luna(max) 52 -- statistically level. This is what you must run locally to claim you have matched Luna.

qwen3.8-27b.source: https://www.yottalabs.ai/post/qwen-3-8-27b-specs-hardware-requirements-how-to-run-2026 ; https://benchlm.ai/models/qwen3-8-27b ; weights on HF under Apache 2.0
qwen3.8-27b.note: THE CONSUMER-SCALE CAPABILITY MATCH, and a much closer one than V4 Flash: SWE-Bench Pro 61.7 vs Luna's 62.7. DENSE, not MoE -- Qwen 3.8-Max is the sparse one at ~95B active. Luna still leads on knowledge breadth (GPQA 92.3; the previous-gen Qwen3.6-27B lost GPQA, MMMU-Pro and SWE-Bench Pro to Luna outright) and on context (1.05M vs 262K). Gated DeltaNet's linear attention makes the KV cache far cheaper than a standard 27B, which is what makes long context on 32 GB thinkable at all.
qwen3.8-27b.bits_note: 4.25 effective bits assumes NVFP4 MoE-style weight quant with norms/embeddings/router left higher. Drives weights_gb, which drives the decode roofline, so it is load-bearing.

deepseek-v4-flash-0731.note: NOT a capability match for Luna. Luna beats it 92.3 vs 71.2 GPQA, 62.7 vs 49.1 SWE-bench Pro, 84.7 vs 49.1 Terminal-Bench 2.0. Included because it is the honest cheap fallback if sovereignty, not parity, is the actual requirement.

sources: throughput: https://inferencex.semianalysis.com/compare/deepseek-v4-b200-vs-gb200 (B200 976 tok/s/GPU @105 tok/s/user on V4 Pro 1.6T)
power: HGX B200 8-GPU ~10.2 kW typical, ~12 kW at 8x1000W TDP, DGX B200 ~14.3 kW max incl. cooling
price: https://www.mercatus-ai.com/blog/b200-server-price ($400-500k, ~$450k typical integrated quote; DGX B200 lists ~$515k)
8xB200-HGX.it_idle_kw_note: ESTIMATED, not measured: ~150 W/GPU parked + ~1.5 kW host. Lowest-confidence number in this file. Idle draw sets the floor cost of a box that is up 24/7 and busy 10-15% of the time, so it matters here more than it usually would.
8xB200-HGX.pue_note: 1.30 assumes a competent air-cooled enterprise room or colo. An office-building server closet is 1.4-1.5. NVIDIA states liquid cooling is effectively mandatory above ~1000 W/GPU.

sources: power: 120 kW nominal, 130-132 kW observed at full load; https://www.nvidia.com/en-us/data-center/gb200-nvl72/ and https://newsletter.semianalysis.com/p/h100-vs-gb200-nvl72-training-benchmarks
GB200-NVL72.note: Reference rack for the FIRST-PASS question (raw energy per token at scale). Wildly over-provisioned for an 800-seat office; kept so the two framings can be compared in one place. it_idle_kw is a guess.

sources: 96 GB GDDR7, 600 W, 4 PFLOPS peak FP4
12xRTX-PRO-6000-BW.note: SPECULATIVE, no measured V4-Pro throughput exists for this config. 12x96=1152 GB holds the 800 GB weights with room for KV. Capex is ~half the 8xB200. The risk is the interconnect: PCIe 5.0 instead of NVLink, against a 1.6T MoE whose expert parallelism is all-to-all-bound. Decode will suffer, possibly severely. Benchmark before believing. Included so the model can PRICE the option, not so it can recommend it.

sources: 575 W TGP, 580-600 W under heavy load, 32 GB GDDR7, 1,792 GB/s: NVIDIA spec via secondary summaries

street price: https://videocardprices.com/card/nvidia-rtx-5090/ -- US median $4,699.99 Aug 2026, in-stock range $3,900-5,000; $1,999 Founders Edition does not exist at retail, AIB baselines from $2,900
prefill anchor: ~7,200 tok/s on Llama-3.1-8B, via secondary summary
RTX-5090-desktop.capex_note: $6,000 = $4,700 street-median card + ~$1,300 for a 1200 W PSU, CPU, 64 GB RAM, NVMe and case. capex_usd_msrp_era is the same box had the card sold at its $1,999 MSRP -- kept because the shortage roughly DOUBLES the break-even duty cycle, which makes the GPU market a bigger swing factor than electricity or model choice.
RTX-5090-desktop.host_w_note: 90 W CPU is for an inference workload, which barely loads it. Gaming/CPU-offload figures of 'north of 800 W system' assume a loaded CPU and do not apply.
RTX-5090-desktop.no_pue_note: A desktop has no datacenter PUE. It does have summer air conditioning: removing 811 W of heat at COP 3.5 costs another ~232 W. Winter it offsets heating instead. Modelled as an optional multiplier, not baked in.

prefill._note: No published isolated-prefill tok/s exists for V4 Pro. InferenceX publishes decode throughput at fixed interactivity. Prefill is therefore MODELLED, not measured.
prefill.flops_per_token_note: 2 x active_params. Ignores attention FLOPs, which V4's Compressed Sparse Attention + Heavily Compressed Attention make cheap at short context but NOT at 1M. Long-context input costs materially more than this model says -- note OpenAI charges 2x for Luna's long-context tier for the same reason.
prefill.mfu_note: LOWEST-CONFIDENCE NUMBER IN THE MODEL. 30% is a plausible large-MoE prefill MFU, not a measurement. The 20-35% band is carried through every output. Sanity check that it is not absurd: at 30% it implies prefill is ~4x cheaper per token than decode at the 105 tok/s/user operating point, and the measured decode point itself back-solves to ~7% MFU, which is normal for GEMV-bound decode.

api_prices_usd_per_mtok._note: Confirmed by the requester 2026-08-15: the $0.22 originally supplied was AWS Bedrock; OpenAI direct is $0.20, and a batch tier is available at $0.10 input.

luna_direct.source: post-80%-cut pricing, eff. 2026-07-30; launch pricing was $1/$6. Cache: 90% discount on reads, writes at 1.25x uncached input, 30-min minimum cache life, explicit breakpoints
luna_direct.cache_note: Because writes carry a 1.25x premium, caching only pays above a hit rate of (0.25-0.20)/(0.25-0.02) = 21.7%. Below that, re-sending is cheaper than caching.

luna_batch.note: output half-price is INFERRED from the standard 50% batch convention, not confirmed. Only the $0.10 input was given.

workload._note: THE WEAKEST PART OF THE MODEL, and the part you should replace first with real telemetry. Requester's brief: ~800 users, office work, power-curve activity distribution, predominantly M-F 40h weeks with staggered starts (07:00 to 09:30), no meaningful off-hours load except a 2-3 h nightly batch.
workload.peak_hour_request_share_note: Fraction of a day's requests landing in the busiest hour. This is how the power-curve distribution enters the model: it drives PEAK SIZING. It barely moves annual totals.
workload.scenario_provenance: AUTHORED, not sourced. Published per-seat figures found (FinOps LLM: 'light analyst' 3M input tok/day) are ~7x above even scenario C per active user and are not credible for office work; they were rejected rather than used. Scenarios A-C are bracketing guesses. Replace with telemetry.

hourly._note: Single-GPU, per-hour framing -- `hourly.py`. Different question from the fleet model: not 'do we buy a cluster for 800 seats' but 'is one card cheaper than the API while it is running'. Same price book, same electricity rates.
hourly.nominal_decode_note: USER-SUPPLIED PREMISE (180-200 TPS), retained deliberately. It sits ~1.9x above the plain single-stream decode roofline for this model -- see `hourly.py::roofline`. Reachable via the multi-token prediction this model ships, or speculative decoding, or 2+ concurrent streams; NOT reachable by plain decode. `conservative_decode_tok_s` is the roofline-respecting branch and every output is reported at both.
hourly.mbu_note: Memory-bandwidth utilisation for single-stream decode. 0.80 is typical for a well-tuned llama.cpp/vLLM run.
hourly.profiles_provenance: AUTHORED. Ratios and hit rates are bracketing guesses, not telemetry. `bulk` deliberately has use_cache=false because its 10% hit rate is BELOW the 21.7% break-even -- caching it would cost more, which is the point of carrying that row.
hourly.ac_note: Summer only, and only if the box lives in conditioned space. Off by default.
hourly.duty_cycle_note: 'Flat-out generation', not 'hours with the tool open'. Interactive chat generates tokens perhaps 5-10% of wall-clock time, so 4 h/day of real generation is ~1.8M output tokens/day -- an always-on agent or a batch pipeline, not a person typing. Conflating the two is the easiest way to talk yourself into the purchase.

selfhost_opex._note: Everything that is not the box and not the electrons.
selfhost_opex.ops_note: colo or room buildout amortized, network, spares, and 0.3-0.5 FTE of MLOps to keep a production service up for 800 employees. AUTHORED estimate. Set to 0 to see the hardware+power-only floor.
selfhost_opex.redundancy_note: All figures are for ONE node. Serving 800 employees from a single box means one hardware failure removes the company's AI. N+1 doubles capex. The model does NOT include this by default -- multiply capex by 2 to see it.
